title: The Personal Macro Workbook and cleaning up
summary: Macros you want in every workbook go in the Personal Macro Workbook, PERSONAL.XLSB, which opens hidden with Excel. Recorded code works but is wordy: delete the Selects, the settings you didn’t change, and replace fixed ranges with ranges that grow.
objectives: Store a macro in the Personal Macro Workbook and run it from any workbook.
Read recorded code: Sub, comments, Select and Selection.
Shorten recorded code by acting on ranges directly and deleting unchanged settings.
Replace a fixed range with CurrentRegion so the macro works on any number of rows.

p: Choose Store macro in: Personal Macro Workbook, and Excel creates a hidden workbook called PERSONAL.XLSB. It opens every time Excel starts, so its macros are in the Macros list whichever workbook you’re in.
It’s yours, on this computer: colleagues don’t get it.
When you close Excel, it asks to save PERSONAL.XLSB: say **Save**.
To edit it, open the VBE: it’s listed as VBAProject (PERSONAL.XLSB). View › Unhide shows the workbook.
In real life: keeps InsertCompanyName and his number-format macros in PERSONAL.XLSB: they work in every file he opens.

items: Store macro in: Personal Macro Workbook
a hidden workbook in your XLSTART folder

p: Macros that belong to one workbook, like a report’s formatting, stay in that workbook, so they travel with it. Macros you use everywhere, like inserting the company name, go in PERSONAL.XLSB.
Sending a workbook? Its own macros go with it; PERSONAL.XLSB’s don’t.
A button in a shared workbook that calls a PERSONAL.XLSB macro breaks on other people’s computers.
In real life: got Arjun’s file, clicked a button, and saw “Cannot run the macro”. It was in his PERSONAL.XLSB.

check.q: Arjun wants InsertCompanyName in every workbook he opens. He stores it in…

p: Alt+F11 opens the editor. A macro is a Sub: Sub, its name, brackets, the steps, End Sub. Green lines starting with an apostrophe are comments. Then the recorder’s favourite pair: select something, then do something to the Selection.
Read it top to bottom: that’s the order it runs.
Every `.Select` moves the cursor, which is slow and flickers.
Most `With Selection.Interior` lines repeat settings you never changed.
In real life: printed his first recorded macro and highlighted each pair. It read like his own clicks.

visual.text:
Sub FormatReport()
'
' FormatReport Macro
'
    Range("A1:H1").Select
    Selection.Font.Bold = True
    With Selection.Interior
        .Pattern = xlSolid
        .PatternColorIndex = xlAutomatic
        .Color = 16247773
        .TintAndShade = 0
        .PatternTintAndShade = 0
    End With
    Range("G2:H13").Select
    Selection.NumberFormat = "#,##0"
    Range("A1:H13").Select
    Selection.Borders.LineStyle = xlContinuous
    Range("A1").Select
End Sub
notes: Sub, the name, (): the start of the macro
' starts a comment: green, ignored when it runs

p: Select then Selection dot something is the same as acting on the range directly. Join each pair into one line, delete settings you didn’t change, and delete the last Select that just parks the cursor.
`Range("A1:H1").Select` + `Selection.Font.Bold = True` → `Range("A1:H1").Font.Bold = True`.
A With Selection.Interior block with only `.Color` changed → `Range("A1:H1").Interior.Color = 16247773`.
Run it after every change to check it still works.
In real life: noticed the cleaned-up macro no longer flickers across the screen.

p: The recorder wrote A1:H13 because today there were twelve orders. Tomorrow there are fourteen, and the last two get no borders. Range("A1").CurrentRegion is the whole block of data around A1, however many rows it has.
**CurrentRegion** stops at the first completely empty row and column, like Ctrl+A.
It’s the quickest fix for recorded macros; Module 3 finds the last row in other ways.
This is the recorder’s limit: it can’t loop, decide or ask. Writing VBA starts in Module 2.
In real life: tested his macro with 12 rows, and it failed with 14 the next day. Now he tests with a longer copy too.

terms: the block of filled cells around a cell, up to the first empty row and column

visual.text:
Sub FormatReport()
    Range("A1:H1").Font.Bold = True
    Range("A1:H1").Interior.Color = 16247773
    Range("A1").CurrentRegion.Columns("G:H").NumberFormat = "#,##0"
    Range("A1").CurrentRegion.Borders.LineStyle = xlContinuous
End Sub
notes: CurrentRegion: the block around A1; .Columns("G:H") of it
Borders on the whole block, today and tomorrow

lab.intro: Arjun recorded **FormatReport** yesterday (it’s in **Module1**). Clean it up so it’s short and works on any number of orders, then record a macro for every workbook.

tasks.prompt: Clean up **FormatReport**: no `Select` or `Selection` left, and it must still format the sheet exactly as before.
hints: Join each Select / Selection pair: Range("A1:H1").Font.Bold = True.
The fill: Range("A1:H1").Interior.Color = 16247773. Delete the last Range("A1").Select.
tasks.explain: Four lines instead of eighteen, and no flicker.

points: **PERSONAL.XLSB** holds macros for every workbook on your computer; workbook macros travel with the file.
A macro is `Sub Name()` … `End Sub`; `'` starts a comment.
Clean recorded code: join **Select / Selection** pairs, delete unchanged settings.
Replace fixed ranges with **`Range("A1").CurrentRegion`** so tomorrow’s rows are included.
recap.cheat: Personal for you, workbook for the file; no Select; CurrentRegion grows.

cards.back: **PERSONAL.XLSB**: hidden, opens with Excel; its macros work in every workbook on your computer.
They move the cursor: slower, flickers, and not needed to change a range.
Starts with an apostrophe `'`; shown in green; ignored when the macro runs.
